claim: B-SOiD's clustered spatiotemporal features are used to train a Random Forest classifier to detect behavioral classes with millisecond precision.
source: Clustered spatiotemporal features are then used to train a classifier (Random Forest; Breiman, 2001) to detect behavioral classes in data sets that were not used to train the model and with millisecond precision.
evidence: Supported by citation to Random Forest algorithm.

claim: VAME uses self-supervised deep learning models to infer the full range of behavioral dynamics based on the animal movements from pose data.
source: VAME (Luxem et al., 2022a; Luxem et al., 2022b) uses self-supervised deep learning models to infer the full range of behavioral dynamics based on the animal movements from pose data.
evidence: Supported by citations to VAME papers.

claim: VAME uses a variational autoencoder framework to learn a generative model.
source: The variational autoencoder framework (Kingma and Welling, 2019) is used to learn a generative model.
evidence: Supported by citation to variational autoencoder framework.

claim: TREBA relates measures from pose estimation to other quantitative or qualitative data associated with each frame in a video recording.
source: TREBA (Sun et al., 2021c; Sun et al., 2021d) relates measures from pose estimation to other quantitative or qualitative data associated with each frame in a video recording.
evidence: Supported by citations to TREBA papers.

claim: TREBA can incorporate behavioral attributes into representations of the pose estimation data learned by its neural networks using a technique called task programming.
source: TREBA can then incorporate behavioral attributes, such as movement speed, distance traveled, and heuristic labels for behavior (e.g., sniffing, mounting, attacking) into representations of the pose estimation data learned by its neural networks, thereby bringing aspects of supervised learning. This is achieved using a technique called task programming.
evidence: This describes TREBA's technical approach.

claim: SimBA was developed for studies in social behavior and aggression and has been shown to be able to discriminate between attack, pursuit, and threat behaviors in studies using rats and mice.
source: SimBA (Nilsson et al., 2020a; Nilsson et al., 2020b) is a supervised learning pipeline for importing pose estimation data and a graphical interface for interacting with a popular machine learning algorithm called Random Forest (Breiman, 2001). SimBA was developed for studies in social behavior and aggression and has been shown to be able to discriminate between attack, pursuit, and threat behaviors in studies using rats and mice.
evidence: Supported by citations to SimBA papers.

claim: MARS is a supervised learning pipeline developed for studies of social interaction behaviors in rodents and uses the XGBoost gradient boosting classifier.
source: MARS (Segalin et al., 2021a; Segalin et al., 2021b) is another supervised learning pipeline developed for studies of social interaction behaviors in rodents, such as attacking, mounting, and sniffing, and uses the XGBoost gradient boosting classifier (Chen and Guestrin, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to MARS papers and XGBoost.

claim: A-SOiD is an active-learning algorithm that iteratively combines supervised and unsupervised approaches to reduce the amount of training data required and enable the discovery of additional behavior and structure.
source: Recently, A-SOiD, an active-learning algorithm, iteratively combines these supervised and unsupervised approaches to reduce the amount of training data required and enable the discovery of additional behavior and structure (Schweihoff et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to A-SOiD paper.

claim: There is no common and efficient data format available for tools that enable pose estimation in animal research.
source: First, it is important to point out that there is no common and efficient data format available for tools that enable pose estimation in animal research.
evidence: This is an observation about the current state of the field.

claim: There has been a general lack of direct comparisons of different methods and parameter exploration within a given method on a standard set of videos.
source: Second, there has also been a general lack of direct comparisons of different methods and parameter exploration within a given method on a standard set of videos.
evidence: This is an observation about current research practices.

claim: The choice of deep learning method and specific hyperparameters can affect the structural biases embedded in video data, thereby affecting the effectiveness of a given method.
source: The choice of deep learning method and specific hyperparameters can affect the structural biases embedded in video data, thereby affecting the effectiveness of a given method (Sculley et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sculley et al., 2015.

claim: Certain properties of neural network architectures such as maximum receptive field size can dramatically impact the performance across species owing to the variability in morphological features.
source: For example, in pose estimation, certain properties of neural network architectures such as its maximum receptive field size can dramatically impact the performance across species owing to the variability in morphological features (Pereira et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pereira et al., 2022.

claim: Algorithms that achieve temporal smoothness in pose tracking are crucial for studies of fine motor control.
source: For example, algorithms that achieve temporal smoothness in pose tracking are crucial for studies of fine motor control (Wu et al., 2020), but perhaps not as essential as preventing identity swaps for studies of social behavior (Pereira et al., 2022; Segalin et al., 2021a).
evidence: Supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: Most methods do not report well-calibrated measures of the confidence of model fits or predictions.
source: Another important issue is that most methods do not report well-calibrated measures of the confidence of model fits or predictions.
evidence: This is an observation about current method limitations.

claim: Machine learning tools tend to be overconfident in their predictions.
source: This is important as it has become clear that machine learning tools tend to be overconfident in their predictions (Abdar et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Abdar et al., 2021.
